body:
# Independent audit: strict inverse-power radial rigidity and depth equality


`candidate 07f233a26b321ff2`.

ordinary full-dimensional continuous theorem. No borderline exponent,
one-dimensional, lower-rank, or mixed-integer classification is inferred.

## 1. Analytic input and strict quantile equality

I checked the cited Ball proof in Section 1 of
`candidate 2338b9b22d6faa2f`. It supplies
finite positive ray integrals in every direction, their continuity,
a positive global lower bound on the inverse-power function, and an
integrable radial majorant after translation to an interior point.
Along any ray the positive support is an interval beginning at zero.
Its density is positive continuous in the open interval, so the
increasing radial probability quantile is C^1 for 0<v<1, with
positive derivative. Infinite terminal endpoints are allowed.

For an actual boundary point x of the Ball body, the ray integral
is 1/r. Multiplying f by r makes it one. In this temporary
normalization the inverse-power function is also multiplied by
r^(-1/beta); X and Y in the quantile proof are values of that
rescaled inverse-power function. Returning to the original f at
the end gives precisely normalization (2). This scaling changes
neither convexity nor any equality criterion.

With the notation of the source, direct differentiation gives

    T'=T[a X^beta/R_1^r+b Y^beta/R_2^r],
    T=aR_1+bR_2,
    Tz=a R_1 x_1+b R_2 x_2.

Thus convexity of the inverse-power function gives the first
inequality in (3) with its exact exponent and factor T^r. Weighted
Hölder gives

    (aX+bY)^beta
       <=(a X^beta/R_1^r+b Y^beta/R_2^r)
          (a R_1^s+b R_2^s)^(beta-1),
    s=r/(beta-1).

Since beta>r+1, 0<s<1. Strict concavity gives
a R_1^s+b R_2^s<T^s whenever R_1 differs from R_2, and a,b are
strictly positive throughout (0,1). The last lower bound in (3)
is therefore strictly greater than one at every such parameter.
Continuity makes any failure of equality persist on a nonempty
interval, so it produces a strictly positive integrated excess.

The change of variables in this strictness step is valid. T is
strictly increasing from zero, and Tz stays in the open support by
convexity. Its limiting endpoint cannot exceed the positive ray
endpoint in direction z. Integrating covers an initial portion
of that ray; any omitted remaining mass is nonnegative. Thus a
strict excess would contradict the known TOTAL integral one on
the facet ray z, regardless of finite or infinite endpoints.
There is no inference of strictness from an unattained supremum.

Consequently the two quantiles agree at every v. Their probability
laws, terminal endpoints, and ray densities agree. Continuity in
the positive interval upgrades the density equality to pointwise
profile equality there. Continuity at the interior origin supplies
the common t=0 value. Support endpoints may have different assigned
boundary values, which are irrelevant to the measure and are not
used in the quantile identities.

## 2. Facet propagation and the profile's necessary monotonicity

The quantile argument applies to any two distinct points of one
facet. Such a facet is positive-dimensional when r>=2, and it does
not contain the origin. The finite facet-intersection graph is
connected: otherwise its component unions would be disjoint
nonempty compact sets partitioning the boundary, whereas radial
projection identifies that boundary with the connected sphere.
A common point of intersecting facets identifies their ray laws.
Therefore all boundary rays have one common profile and one common
positive endpoint R. This proves the gauge representation on the
entire positive interior and vanishing outside its closure.
The remaining support boundary is Lebesgue-null.

Convexity of h=F^(-1/beta) along a fixed ray is immediate. The
additional monotonicity is correctly PROVED, not presumed from
convexity: for s<t<R, a point of sB lies in tB; the latter is the
convex hull of its scaled vertices, each with the identical
inverse-power value h(t). Convexity therefore gives h(s)<=h(t).
This argument includes s=0 and requires no symmetry. The original
radial definition gives r integral t^(r-1) F(t) dt=1 exactly.

In r=1, the two facets are isolated and the boundary sphere is
disconnected; the propagation step would fail. At beta=r+1 the
power s equals one and the decisive strict concavity disappears.
The source explicitly excludes both cases and makes no equality
claim for them.

## 3. The exact ordinary maximal-depth classification

The attained deepest point and finite positively balanced active
cap cover are supplied by the independently proved inverse-power
depth theorem. At a point of depth Gamma_r, the Ball body preserves
all through-point cap masses and total mass. The finite active
halfspaces cover all of R^r and have body volume Gamma_r|B|.
Consequently every candidate point of B is in a cap of that mass,
giving maximal ordinary depth at most Gamma_r. Ordinary Grünbaum
gives the reverse inequality. The audited ordinary minimum-maximal
depth rigidity theorem applies to this actual full-dimensional
convex Ball body and makes it a simplex.

The origin has depth Gamma_r in B by the full through-origin mass
identity. A simplex has no other deepest point: away from its
centroid at least one barycentric coordinate exceeds 1/(r+1),
and its vertex-side cap has strictly smaller fraction. Thus the
Ball simplex is centered at its centroid. Section 1 of the source
now yields the required profile. No classification of only the
chosen cap-normal span is substituted for the full-dimensional
Ball-body classification.

Conversely, for an integrable gauge profile on a centroid-centered
simplex, polar integration factors the ray integral as its radial
constant times the simplex radius to the power r. Every through-
origin halfspace therefore has exactly its uniform-simplex mass
fraction. Grünbaum gives depth Gamma_r at the origin, while the
r+1 canonical through-origin vertex halfspaces cover all of R^r
and each has that same profile mass fraction. This bounds every
candidate point from above, proving equality of MAXIMAL depth,
not only equality at the selected origin. Monotonicity/convexity
of the profile gives class membership; the angular sufficiency
argument itself only requires its positive finite radial integral.

## 4. Log-concavity and measure conventions

For an integrable log-concave density, exp((-log f)/beta) is convex
on its convex positive interior for every beta>0. Assigning the
extended value +infinity outside that interior is a convex extension;
changing support-boundary values changes no Lebesgue integrals.
Choose any beta>r+1 and apply the proved strict theorem. Repeating
the ray and scaled-vertex argument with -log f gives precisely a
convex nondecreasing scalar h. Conversely h composed with a convex
gauge is convex, so the asserted profile is log-concave. The finite
or infinite radial support endpoint is handled by the same extended
convex convention.

All measures here are ordinary r-dimensional Lebesgue density
measures. Hyperplanes and convex support boundaries are null;
there is no discrete fiber sum, lattice normalization, or selected
mixed-integer center in the argument. The proof contains no
unclaimed extension to beta=r+1 or to rank-deficient projected
equality families. No substantive correction was needed.
